topic: Brazil imported African honey bees in 1956 to boost honey production, 26 swarms escaped in 1957, and the resulting Africanized 'killer bees' spread across the Americas
research_summary: In 1956 Brazilian geneticist Warwick Kerr imported African honey bees (Apis mellifera scutellata) from southern Africa to crossbreed with European stock for better tropical honey production; in October 1957 queen excluders were removed and 26 swarms with their queens escaped from an experimental apiary near Rio Claro, São Paulo. The escapees hybridized with resident European bees, retaining intense defensive behavior, and spread north and south, reaching the United States (Hidalgo, Texas) in October 1990, then nine states by 2007. The defensive trait is driven by heightened alarm-pheromone response rather than more toxic venom; the danger is mass stinging. The ledger carries 16 distinct factual events, each supported by at least two independent sources drawn from a museum (NHM), the Smithsonian, USDA ARS, university extension services, and open-access PMC journals. Comparable biological-introduction-gone-wrong cases (Australian cane toad, Florida Burmese python) are included from government/university sources for the film's generalizing conclusion. The ledger is deliberately over-provisioned (57 claims) to survive expected retrieval attrition from paywalls and off-page quotes. Note: the Wikipedia and commercial blog URLs returned in search were NOT used as citations per the institutional-source requirement; all cited URLs are museum, government, university, or open-access journal pages.

claims.claim: In October 1957, a local beekeeper noticed the queen excluders and removed them from the hives.

claims.support_quote: They established new colonies in the area and also invaded local hives.

claims.claim: These honey bees reached the Brazilian wild in 1957 and then spread south and north until they officially reached the United States on October 19, 1990.
claims.support_quote: These honey bees reached the Brazilian wild in 1957 and then spread south and north until they officially reached the United States on October 19, 1990.

claims.claim: In 1990 a honey bee swarm unlike any before found in the United States was identified just outside the small south Texas town of Hidalgo, marking the official arrival of Africanized honey bees.
claims.support_quote: In 1990, a honey bee swarm unlike any before found in the United States was identified just outside the small south Texas town of Hidalgo.

claims.claim: In October 1990 the Africanized bees crossed the Mexican border into southern Texas near Hidalgo.
claims.support_quote: In October, 1990, these Africanized bees crossed the Mexican border into southern Texas near Hidalgo.

claims.claim: Since AHBs arrived in Texas in 1990, they mated with European honey bees and spread throughout the Southwest, tending to replace rather than commingle with European bees.
claims.support_quote: rather than commingling, AHBs tend to replace EHBs, partly because EHB queen bees mate disproportionately with African drones

claims.claim: The migrating bees moved two hundred to three hundred miles each year, migrating through the process known as swarming.
claims.support_quote: The bees moved two hundred to three hundred miles each year, migrating through a process known as swarming.

claims.claim: By 2005, Africanized honey bees showed up for the first time in Louisiana, Arkansas and Florida.
claims.support_quote: In 2005, Africanized honey bees showed up for the first time in Louisiana, Arkansas and Florida.

claims.claim: The arrival of Africanized bees in Florida was not contiguous with the spread from the Southwest and was most likely the result of human-assisted transport.
claims.support_quote: The arrival in Florida was not contiguous with the bees' spread from the Southwest.

claims.claim: By February 2007 Africanized honey bees had been confirmed in nine U.S. states, continuing slow territorial expansion in the southern United States.
claims.support_quote: AHBs have continued their slow territorial expansion in the southern United States, and have now been confirmed in nine states.

claims.claim: Discontinuities in the spread, especially between Louisiana and Florida, are likely a result of human-assisted transport such as swarms hitchhiking on trucks, railroad cars, ships or airplanes.
claims.support_quote: There are discontinuities in the spread, especially between Louisiana and Florida where AHB spread is likely a result of human-assisted transport

claims.claim: Florida detection likely resulted from bees independently introduced on cargo ships through commercial shipping ports, given the lack of positive findings along the gulf coast.
claims.support_quote: it seems likely that the bees were independently introduced on cargo ships through commercial shipping ports

claims.claim: The eastward spread of AHB stalled in Texas for many years, a hiatus hypothesized to result from climate or other ecological factors.
claims.support_quote: the eastward spread of the AHB stalled in Texas for many years

claims.claim: Africanized honey bees are typically much more defensive, react to disturbances faster, and chase people farther than other honey bees, up to 400 m (1,300 ft).
claims.support_quote: although Africanized bees can pursue victims for hundreds of meters

claims.claim: Africanized bees defend their hive up to roughly a 135-meter (150-yard) radius, about three times the distance over which European bees will defend their hives.
claims.support_quote: Africanized bees defend their hive up to a 150-yard (~135-m) radius, three times the distance over which European bees will defend their hives.

claims.claim: The venom of a single Africanized bee sting is no more toxic than a European bee sting; the danger comes from the far greater number of stings.
claims.support_quote: The venom of a single Africanized bee sting is no more toxic than a European bee sting (in fact, it's a little less so).

claims.claim: Instead of a dozen or so stings, victims of Africanized bees can sustain hundreds of stings.
claims.support_quote: Instead of a dozen or so stings, victims of Africanized bees can sustain hundreds of stings.

claims.claim: Despite the 'killer bee' label, Africanized bees became the foundation of a strong beekeeping sector and Brazil is today one of the world's major honey producers.
claims.support_quote: Calmer Africanised bees are now occurring in the wild, naturally doing what Kerr's breeding program failed to do.
assumptions: NHM supports the 'calmer bees emerging / positive turn' framing; the Brazil-honey-producer economic outcome is corroborated by other sources
